common_name: Orchid Frost Lamium (Silver-Leaved Lavender-Pink Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Orchid Frost bears nearly solid silver leaves with a narrow green margin and clear lavender-pink flowers, and is notably more vigorous and mildew-resistant than older Lamium cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which scorches the pale foliage. Orchid Frost bears striking, nearly solid silver leaves edged with a narrow band of green, among the brightest foliage of any Lamium cultivar, topped by clear lavender-pink flowers from late spring into summer, and shows improved vigor and resistance to the powdery mildew that troubles older, less-refined Lamium selections. It spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, quickly knitting together a dense, weed-suppressing, low groundcover beneath trees and shrubs, brightening dark corners of the shade garden with its luminous foliage even when not in bloom. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to encourage fresh growth and tidy the mat, and divide congested patches in spring if increase or containment is needed.

common_name: Pink Pewter Lamium (Pewter-Silver Soft Pink Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Pink Pewter bears pewter-silver foliage with a thin green edge and soft, pale pink flowers, forming a tidy, non-aggressive mat.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which scorches the pale foliage. Pink Pewter bears soft, silvery pewter-toned leaves with a thin green margin, a gentler, more muted metallic look than the brighter silver 'Orchid Frost', paired with delicate, soft pink flowers from late spring into summer. Its habit is tidy and relatively restrained compared to more aggressive Lamium selections, making it well suited to smaller shaded beds or mixed woodland plantings without overwhelming neighbors. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense, weed-suppressing low groundcover beneath trees and shrubs. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to encourage fresh growth, and divide congested patches in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Golden Anniversary Lamium (Gold-Edged Silver-Striped Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Golden Anniversary bears green leaves broadly edged in gold with a silver center stripe, a brighter, warmer variegation than solid-silver Lamium cultivars, useful for lighting up deep shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun, which scorches the variegated foliage. Golden Anniversary bears distinctively three-toned leaves, a broad golden-yellow margin surrounding a central silvery stripe over green, a warmer, brighter variegation pattern than the solid-silver Lamium cultivars more commonly grown, paired with lavender-pink flowers from late spring into summer. The gold edging is especially effective at lighting up deep or dry shade beneath trees, where its glow reads clearly even in low light. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover. Shear lightly after the main flush of bloom to encourage fresh growth, and divide congested patches in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Bronze Beauty Ajuga (Classic Glossy Coppery-Bronze Bugleweed)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile soil in full shade to part shade; Bronze Beauty is a classic ajuga selection with glossy, coppery-bronze foliage and blue flower spikes, distinct from tricolor and near-black ajuga cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; ajuga is one of the most reliable and ornamental groundcovers for shaded areas under trees and along shaded borders. Bronze Beauty is a classic, long-cultivated ajuga selection bearing glossy, rounded leaves in a rich, uniform coppery-bronze, a simpler, more solid-colored counterpart to the mottled tricolor and near-black ajuga cultivars more recently introduced, topped in spring by short spikes of deep blue flowers. It spreads by stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat that tolerates foot traffic reasonably well and thrives in the dry shade beneath established trees where turf grass struggles. Divide and thin congested patches every few years to maintain vigor and prevent crown rot in overly wet or crowded conditions.

common_name: Metallica Crispa Ajuga (Crinkled Metallic Bronze-Purple Clump-Forming Bugle)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Metallica Crispa bears crinkled, metallic bronze-purple, crimped foliage on a clumping, non-running habit, distinct from stoloniferous Ajuga reptans cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade. Metallica Crispa is a striking dwarf bugle species distinct from the common creeping Ajuga reptans, growing as a tight, non-running clump rather than spreading by stolons, with unusual, deeply crimped and crinkled leaves in a lustrous metallic bronze-purple that catches the light, topped by short spikes of blue flowers in spring. Its clumping habit and small scale make it well suited to a shaded rock garden, trough, or the front edge of a woodland border where a spreading groundcover would be unwelcome. Water during dry spells and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted, though it spreads far more slowly than typical creeping ajuga.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this barren-strawberry relative bears rounder, more scalloped leaves and yellow flowers than the more commonly grown Waldsteinia ternata, and forms a clump rather than a fast-running mat.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. This barren-strawberry species bears attractive, rounded, scalloped leaves resembling strawberry foliage and small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers in spring, closely related to but distinct in leaf shape and growth habit from the more commonly grown Waldsteinia ternata, forming a neat, well-behaved clump that spreads more slowly and stays better contained than its faster-running relative. It makes a durable, low-maintenance groundcover for the shaded border, tolerating dry shade once established and requiring essentially no care beyond an occasional trim to keep edges tidy. Divide clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to poor soil in full to deep shade; Variegated Goutweed bears crisp white-margined leaves that brighten deep, dry shade where little else thrives, and young spring shoots have historically been eaten as a pot-herb. Site with care, since it spreads aggressively by rhizomes and is best confined to contained or difficult sites.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, and choose the planting site with care, since Variegated Goutweed spreads vigorously and persistently by rhizomes and can be difficult to remove once established; it is best used in a contained bed, a hard-to-plant difficult site such as under a deck or between buildings, or bordered by pavement or a buried barrier. Its crisply white-margined, green-centered leaves brighten deep, dry shade far better than most groundcovers tolerate, forming a dense, weed-suppressing carpet that spreads where turf and most perennials fail to grow. Small white flower umbels appear in early summer but are usually removed before seed sets, since the variegated form can occasionally revert to the more aggressive plain-green species. Historically, young spring shoots were gathered and cooked as a pot-herb similar to spinach, though the plant is grown today almost exclusively as an ornamental groundcover.

common_name: Variegated Creeping Broadleaf Sedge (Cream-Striped Deciduous Woodland Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this creamy white-striped form of the broad, grass-unlike Japanese and Korean woodland sedge is a slow-spreading deciduous groundcover.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Unlike most sedges, this species bears broad, lance-shaped, distinctly grass-unlike leaves, and the Variegata form brightens the woodland floor with crisp creamy-white longitudinal stripes running the length of each leaf, spreading slowly by rhizomes to form a low, deciduous groundcover that dies back in winter and re-emerges fresh each spring. It combines well with hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials, providing a fine-textured, brightly variegated foil for bolder foliage nearby. Water during dry spells, since it prefers consistent moisture over drought, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Marginata Greater Woodrush (Cream-Edged Dry-Shade Evergreen Woodrush)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Marginata bears narrow cream leaf margins and thrives in deep, dry shade where turf and many other groundcovers fail.

directions: Plant in average to humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; greater woodrush is exceptionally tolerant of dry, root-filled shade, thriving beneath established trees where grass and many other groundcovers give up. Marginata bears broad, glossy, evergreen grass-like leaves edged in a narrow band of creamy white, a subtle brightening effect that shows well against darker foliage nearby, and produces airy, brown-bronze flower clusters on wiry stems in late spring. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen groundcover, and is one of the most reliable and low-maintenance choices for difficult dry shade. Cut back tattered old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Aurea Greater Woodrush (Golden-Yellow Winter-Brightening Evergreen Woodrush)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Aurea bears golden-yellow evergreen foliage that becomes most vivid in winter cold, tolerant of the deep, dry shade where turf and many groundcovers fail.

directions: Plant in average to humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; greater woodrush is exceptionally tolerant of dry, root-filled shade, thriving beneath established trees where grass and many other groundcovers give up. Aurea bears broad, glossy, grass-like evergreen leaves in a warm golden-yellow that intensifies to its most vivid color during the cold months, providing valuable winter color in the shaded garden when most perennials are dormant, and softens to chartreuse-green through the growing season. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen groundcover, and produces airy, bronze flower clusters on wiry stems in late spring. Cut back tattered old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in spring if increase is wanted.

common_name: Black Sedge (Blue-Green Foliage Near-Black-Spiked Wetland-Edge Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Sedge is a European wetland-edge species with blue-green foliage and near-black flower spikes, tolerant of partial shade and useful along pond and stream margins.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Sedge tolerates standing water for periods and is well suited to pond margins, stream banks, rain gardens, and other consistently damp sites. It forms a fine-textured clump of narrow, blue-green foliage topped in late spring by distinctive, near-black flower spikes, a striking dark accent among the mostly green- or gold-toned sedges more commonly planted. As a European wetland-edge native, it tolerates a range of light conditions from full sun to partial shade, making it a versatile choice for the damp, dappled-light edges of a woodland pond or rain garden. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: White Beauty Fawn Lily (Large Recurved White Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; White Beauty is a superior selection with larger, recurved white flowers with maroon-ringed centers and heavily mottled leaves.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it. White Beauty is a superior named selection of the California fawn lily, bearing larger, gracefully recurved white flowers marked with a distinctive maroon-brown ring at the throat, held above handsomely mottled, brown-and-green marbled leaves, one of the showiest and most sought-after selections in the genus. It naturalizes gradually in a cool, humus-rich woodland setting beneath deciduous trees, going summer-dormant after flowering. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs. Once established, it requires minimal care and slowly increases into an attractive spring-blooming colony.

common_name: Tuolumne Fawn Lily (Vigorous Bright-Yellow Plain-Leaf Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Tuolumne Fawn Lily bears vigorous bright-yellow flowers over plain, glossy, unmottled leaves, distinct from the mottled-leaf trout lily species more commonly grown.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it. Native to the Sierra Nevada foothills of California, Tuolumne Fawn Lily is distinguished from most other Erythronium species by its plain, glossy green, unmottled leaves rather than the brown-marbled foliage typical of the genus, and it is also one of the most vigorous and easily grown species, readily multiplying by offsets to form an increasing clump of bright, clear yellow, backswept flowers in early spring. It naturalizes well in a cool, humus-rich woodland setting beneath deciduous trees and is often used as a parent in Erythronium hybrid breeding for its vigor. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

common_name: Flore Pleno Double Snowdrop (Layered-Petal Double-Flowered Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Flore Pleno bears a fully double flower with multiple layered inner petals, a historic and long-cultivated form distinct from the single-flowered species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. Flore Pleno, a centuries-old sport of the common snowdrop first recorded in the 1700s, bears a charmingly full, double flower packed with numerous small, ruffled inner petal segments in place of the simple three-part bloom of the wild species, opening in late winter to very early spring as one of the first flowers of the year. It naturalizes gradually into drifts under favorable conditions, multiplying by offset bulbs, and is best left undisturbed once established, dividing and replanting clumps only while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active, for best transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

common_name: S. Arnott Snowdrop (Large Fragrant Vigorous Hybrid Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; S. Arnott bears large, strongly honey-scented flowers on a vigorous hybrid snowdrop widely regarded as one of the best garden snowdrops for reliable increase and flower size.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. S. Arnott, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, is widely regarded by snowdrop growers as one of the finest and most garden-worthy hybrid snowdrops available, bearing unusually large, rounded, pure-white flowers with a strong, sweet honey fragrance, held on tall, sturdy stems well above the foliage, and increasing vigorously and reliably into substantial drifts faster than many named cultivars. It flowers in late winter to very early spring, among the first bulbs of the year. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active, for the most reliable transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

common_name: Robinsoniana Wood Anemone (Lavender-Blue Historic Wood Anemone Selection)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Robinsoniana, one of the oldest and most popular colored selections, bears lavender-blue flowers, distinct from the white species form.

directions: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep, horizontally, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Robinsoniana, one of the oldest and most widely grown colored selections of wood anemone, bears soft lavender-blue flowers with a silvery reverse, a gentle departure from the pure white of the wild species, opening in early to mid spring and closing at night and in overcast weather. Like other wood anemones, it spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form an increasingly dense carpet over the years in a favorable woodland setting, then goes fully dormant by early summer, disappearing until the following spring. It combines beautifully with early daffodils, trilliums, and other spring woodland ephemerals. Once established, it requires essentially no care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

common_name: Vestal Wood Anemone (Fully Double Pure-White Pompon-Centered Anemone)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Vestal bears a fully double, pure white flower with a pompon-like tufted center, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep, horizontally, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees. Vestal, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bears a fully double flower with an outer ring of pure white petals surrounding a dense, tufted, button-like pompon center of smaller white segments, one of the most elegant and sought-after wood anemone forms, opening in early to mid spring and closing at night and in overcast weather. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes to form a gradually increasing carpet in a favorable woodland setting, then goes fully summer-dormant, disappearing until the following spring. It combines beautifully with early daffodils, trilliums, and other spring woodland ephemerals. Once established it requires essentially no care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

common_name: Cilician Cyclamen (Autumn-Winter-Flowering Pale Pink Hardy Cyclamen)

planting.note: Plant tubers in late summer to fall, shallowly, in gritty, well-drained soil in dry shade under trees; Cilician Cyclamen bears smaller, pale-pink flowers with a deeper-pink nose and neatly patterned leaves, blooming in autumn into winter, later than Cyclamen hederifolium.

directions: Plant tubers shallowly, just below the soil surface, in late summer to fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in dry shade beneath trees, where the summer dormancy period stays relatively dry. Cilician Cyclamen, native to mountainous woodland in southern Turkey, bears dainty, pale pink flowers with a deeper pink blotch at the nose in autumn into early winter, blooming somewhat later in the season than the more commonly grown Cyclamen hederifolium, above neat, attractively patterned silver-and-green leaves that persist through winter before going dormant in late spring. It thrives in the same dry shade under mature trees that defeats most other perennials, self-sows gently over time to form a colony, and needs no supplemental water once dormant for summer. Avoid overhead watering during dormancy, since the tubers are prone to rot in consistently wet soil.
